en: The Jātaka:
Miscellaneous Section,
Chapter on the Rice-field of Śāli Rice.
7. The Pañcuposathika Jātaka “Now you may be at ease, O pigeon;
you have no need for food, O bird.”
“Enduring thirst even for the sake of God,
why do you, O pigeon, observe the fast?
“In the past, I was overcome by greed for my female pigeon.”
"In this place we both took delight;
then the fowler seized the female dove,
and I became unwilling to be without her."
Through separation from her various existences,
I experience mind-made feelings;
therefore, I observe the Uposatha.
“O passion, do not come back to me again!
“O serpent with crooked gait, double-tongued,
whose weapon is its fangs, you snake of terrible venom!”
"Enduring even thirst for the sake of the Dhamma,
why indeed, long-lived one, do you observe the Uposatha?
You were once a powerful bull belonging to a village headman."
Like a black snake endowed with color and strength,
he stepped on me; enraged, I bit him,
and overcome by pain, he met his death.
Then the people, having departed from the village,
went away after weeping and wailing;
therefore, I observe the Uposatha.
May anger not come to me again.
There is much flesh of the dead in the charnel ground,
yet that which is pleasing to you in food is but that.
Enduring thirst even for the sake of the Dhamma,
why, O jackal, did you enter the belly of a great elephant while observing the Uposatha?
Delighting in carrion and greedy for the flesh of elephants,
the hot wind and the sharp rays of the sun dried up the path of his dung.
"I am thin and pale, O Venerable One;
there was no path for my departure.
A great cloud suddenly poured down."
Then I shall emerge from that path of charcoal dust, O Blessed One,
like the moon released from the mouth of Rāhu.
Therefore, I observe the Uposatha;
may greed never come to me again.
Like ants upon an anthill, [let them not return].
In the past you used to wander about crushing [beings],
enduring hunger and thirst;
why do you now remain as one observing the Uposatha?
Deeply disparaging my own home,
out of excessive desire I went to the village of Mallagāma;
then, people having emerged from that village,
They crushed me with a bow;
with my head split open and my limbs smeared with blood,
I returned to my own abode.
"Therefore, I shall observe the Uposatha;
do not come back again out of excessive desire.
"That which you asked us, O Blessed One—"
"We have all explained according to our own understanding;
we too ask you, O Blessed One:
Why, Brahmā, are you observing the Uposatha?"
“Unstained, a Paccekabuddha sat for a moment in my hermitage;
he taught me about going and coming.”
His name, his clan, and his entire conduct—
I did not bow at his feet in this manner,
nor did I question him out of pride.
"Therefore, I observe the Uposatha;
let not pride come to me again.
Thus ends the seventh Jātaka, the Pañcuposathika Jātaka.
